In your dating pool, extremely attractive people seem to have worse personalities, and vice versa — even though attractiveness and personality are completely uncorrelated in the general population. What best explains this apparent negative correlation?
choices: Selection bias: you only consider people who clear a minimum combined-desirability bar, so within that selected group, low value in one trait requires high value in the other, creating an artificial negative correlation (Berkson's paradox).
The correlation is real and holds in the general population too, not just your dating pool.
Unattractive people are nicer because they compensate for their looks.
Attractive people become unpleasant because they get away with more.

questions.q: A father leaves 17 camels to his three sons: the eldest gets half, the second gets a third, and the youngest gets a ninth — numbers that don't divide 17 evenly. A wise elder lends them one camel to solve it. What happens?
choices: They now have 18 camels: the sons take 9, 6, and 2 camels respectively (17 total), and the elder takes back the borrowed camel.
The problem has no valid solution and the will is voided by the court.
The 17 camels are simply divided into three equal groups after rounding.
They now have 18 camels: the sons take 9, 6, and 3 camels respectively, and the elder keeps the borrowed camel as payment.

questions.q: Removing one grain of sand from a heap never turns it into a 'non-heap' — one grain can't matter. Repeating this one grain at a time eventually removes the whole heap, yet each step seemed valid. What does this ancient puzzle (the Sorites paradox) actually demonstrate?
choices: That heaps do not really exist as objects.
That mathematical induction is invalid for physical objects.
That the correct definition of a heap is exactly 10,000 grains.
That vague predicates like 'heap' have no sharp boundary, so a chain of individually plausible small steps can lead to an absurd conclusion.
